title: Hardware, Runtime, and Capacity Planning
summary: This intermediate module teaches you to estimate memory demand, design representative runtime measurements, and turn those measurements into a defensible capacity plan. After completing it, you can identify whether model weights, request-dependent state, or observed runtime behavior limits a proposed deployment.
objectives: Calculate a lower bound for model-weight memory from parameter count and storage size per parameter.
Identify persistent, request-dependent, temporary, and runtime-managed memory that a capacity estimate must consider.
Design a representative measurement that records latency, throughput, and peak memory under stated workload conditions.
Use measured limits rather than average utilization alone to decide whether a proposed workload fits available capacity.

sections.title: What changed in this update
paragraphs: The previous source entry was a catalogue-relative JSON path attributed to an unregistered publisher and had never been verified. This update replaces that entry with canonical arXiv records for the transformer architecture and memory management during language-model serving.

The change affects source provenance and the support for claims about attention, autoregressive decoding, and request-dependent memory. The planning method remains provider-neutral and does not introduce a product-specific configuration.

sections.title: Level and scope
paragraphs: This is an intermediate-level module. It assumes that you can rearrange a simple multiplication formula, distinguish bytes from bits, and interpret latency as time per response and throughput as completed work per unit of time. It does not assume experience with a particular hardware vendor, runtime, or hosting provider.

Capacity planning connects a model's static storage requirements with workload-dependent memory and measured runtime behavior. A useful plan separates what can be calculated before deployment from what must be measured in the intended environment.

sections.title: Calculate the weight-memory lower bound
paragraphs: A first estimate for model-weight memory is P × b, where P is the number of stored parameters and b is the number of bytes used to store each parameter. This is a lower bound for the weights themselves, not a complete runtime-memory estimate.

For example, if a model description supplies P and its storage representation establishes b, multiply them and convert the result into the memory unit used by the target environment. Do not guess either value. If the model description does not establish the parameter count or storage representation, the resulting weight-memory requirement is UNKNOWN and should not be asserted.

A model can require more memory at runtime than this lower bound because execution may also retain request-dependent state, temporary working data, and memory managed by the runtime. The exact amount is implementation-dependent and must be measured.

sections.title: Account for request-dependent memory
paragraphs: A transformer decoder generates output while attending to previously available positions. Serving systems can retain key and value data associated with those positions so that later decoding steps can reuse them. This request-dependent state grows with the active sequence data and is not included in the weight-only calculation.

For planning, classify memory into four categories: model weights that persist while the model is loaded, request-dependent state that changes with active sequences, temporary working memory used during computation, and runtime-managed overhead. This classification prevents the weight estimate from being mistaken for total required capacity.

Concurrent requests may have different sequence lengths and may finish at different times. Consequently, total request-dependent memory and the amount of reusable free space can vary during a run. A capacity test should therefore include the expected distribution of input lengths, output lengths, and concurrency rather than testing only one short request.

sections.title: Measure runtime behavior
paragraphs: Record the conditions of every measurement: the model representation, available hardware resources, input-length distribution, requested output-length distribution, concurrency, and the point at which timing begins and ends. Without those conditions, two latency or throughput results may describe different workloads and cannot be compared reliably.

Measure both latency and throughput because they answer different questions. Latency describes how long an individual request or response stage takes. Throughput describes how much work the system completes over time. Increasing concurrent work can improve throughput while also increasing waiting time, so neither metric substitutes for the other.

Record peak memory during the representative run, not only memory observed before requests begin or an average over the run. A deployment must survive its relevant peak. The exact peak, sustainable throughput, and latency are UNKNOWN until they are measured in the intended environment.

sections.title: Build the capacity plan
paragraphs: Begin with the calculated weight-memory lower bound. Add the measured peak contribution from request-dependent state, temporary work, and runtime-managed overhead under a representative workload. Compare the resulting peak with usable capacity in the same units.

Next, run a load test that represents expected request lengths and concurrency. Increase offered work only while recording latency, throughput, failures, and peak memory. The sustainable limit is the highest tested workload that continues to meet the deployment's stated service requirements without exceeding usable capacity.

Do not select a universal utilization percentage without evidence. Required reserve depends on workload variation, failure handling, runtime behavior, and the consequences of exhausting memory or missing a latency target. Choose reserve from measured variability and documented operational requirements, then record the reasoning so the plan can be reviewed.

A complete decision states the assumptions, calculated lower bound, test workload, measured peak memory, measured latency and throughput, acceptance thresholds, and reserve. If any required input or measurement is unavailable, mark that part UNKNOWN and do not claim that the deployment fits.
sections.callout: Estimate static demand first, measure dynamic demand second, and approve capacity only against explicit workload and service requirements.

questions.prompt: Which expression gives the lower bound for memory occupied by model weights?
choices: Parameter count multiplied by bytes stored per parameter
questions.explanation: The module defines the weight-memory lower bound as P × b, where P is parameter count and b is bytes stored per parameter.

questions.prompt: Why is the weight-memory calculation insufficient as a complete runtime-capacity estimate?
choices: It excludes request-dependent state, temporary work, and runtime-managed overhead.
It already includes every possible concurrent request.
It measures latency rather than memory.
It can be used only after a deployment fails.
questions.explanation: The weight calculation covers stored model parameters only. Total runtime memory can also include request-dependent state, temporary working memory, and runtime-managed overhead.

questions.prompt: Which test best supports a deployment-capacity decision?
choices: One short request with no record of its conditions
A representative mix of input lengths, output lengths, and concurrency with latency, throughput, failures, and peak memory recorded
A weight-memory calculation with no runtime measurement
An average-memory reading taken before requests begin
questions.explanation: The module requires representative request lengths and concurrency, together with measurements of latency, throughput, failures, and peak memory.

questions.prompt: What should a planner do when a required model property or runtime measurement is unavailable?
choices: Use a universal default and present it as measured
Mark the value UNKNOWN and avoid claiming that the deployment fits
Ignore the missing value if average utilization is low
Replace peak memory with model-file size
questions.explanation: The module instructs the planner to mark unavailable required inputs or measurements as UNKNOWN and not assert that capacity is sufficient.
